title: SQL
description: Practice SQL on the MySQL Sakila sample database — from SELECT basics to window functions, with hints, explanations, and worked solutions.

roadmap.title: Foundations
roadmap.blurb: Ask the database simple questions. Learn to pick columns, choose rows, and put answers in order.

roadmap.title: Summarizing data
roadmap.blurb: Count, total, and average groups of rows, and tidy up text and dates.

roadmap.title: Combining tables
roadmap.blurb: Connect related tables with JOINs and answer questions with questions using subqueries.

roadmap.title: Changing data
roadmap.blurb: Add, update, and remove rows safely with INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE.

roadmap.title: Speed & structure
roadmap.blurb: Make queries fast with indexes, and reuse logic with views and CTEs.

roadmap.title: Analytics
roadmap.blurb: Rank, run totals, and compare rows to their neighbours with window functions.

topics.title: Basic SELECT
topics.description: Learn the foundations: SELECT, WHERE, LIMIT, ORDER BY, DISTINCT, and column aliases against the Sakila actor, film and customer tables.

questions.question: Which clause retrieves every column from the actor table?
questions.hint: The asterisk is shorthand for 'all columns'.
questions.explanation: SELECT * FROM actor; returns every column for every row. * means 'all columns' in SQL.

questions.question: Which keyword removes duplicate rows from a result set?
questions.explanation: DISTINCT eliminates duplicate rows in the result. Example: SELECT DISTINCT rating FROM film;

questions.question: Which query orders films by length, longest first?
options: SELECT * FROM film SORT BY length DESC;
SELECT * FROM film ORDER BY length ASC;
SELECT * FROM film ORDER BY length DESC;
SELECT * FROM film ORDER length DESC;
questions.explanation: ORDER BY length DESC sorts rows from highest length to lowest. ASC (default) is ascending.

questions.question: Which clause limits the result to the first 10 rows?
questions.hint: MySQL uses a keyword, not TOP.
questions.explanation: MySQL/Sakila uses LIMIT 10 at the end of a query to cap the rows returned.

questions.question: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
questions.hint: One filters individual rows, the other filters groups.
options: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation
WHERE works only with text; HAVING with numbers
questions.explanation: WHERE applies to individual rows before GROUP BY. HAVING applies to aggregated groups produced by GROUP BY.

questions.question: Which alias syntax renames the column first_name to fname?
options: SELECT first_name AS fname FROM actor;
questions.explanation: Use AS to give a column an alias. SELECT first_name AS fname FROM actor; renames first_name to fname in the result.

questions.question: Which query returns the second page (rows 11–20) of films ordered by title?
options: SELECT * FROM film ORDER BY title LIMIT 10;
SELECT * FROM film ORDER BY title LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10;
SELECT * FROM film ORDER BY title PAGE 2;
SELECT * FROM film ORDER BY title LIMIT 20;
questions.explanation: LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10 skips the first 10 rows and returns the next 10. The MySQL shorthand is LIMIT 10, 10.

questions.question: What does SELECT 1 FROM actor; return?
questions.hint: Think about what '1' evaluates to per row.
options: A single row containing the number 1
An error — you cannot SELECT a literal
One row per actor, each containing the number 1
questions.explanation: A literal in the SELECT list is evaluated once per row. So you get N rows of '1', where N = number of actors.

questions.question: Which keyword sorts in descending order?
questions.explanation: DESC tells ORDER BY to sort from highest to lowest. ASC is ascending and is the default.

questions.question: Which clause is used to filter rows in a SELECT?
questions.explanation: WHERE filters rows before grouping or aggregation. Example: SELECT * FROM actor WHERE first_name = 'NICK';

questions.question: Fill in the blank: SELECT first_name, last_name ___ actor;
questions.hint: The clause that names the source table.
questions.explanation: FROM specifies which table the data is being selected from.

questions.question: Which keyword returns only unique values of a column?
questions.explanation: DISTINCT removes duplicates: SELECT DISTINCT rating FROM film; returns each rating once.

questions.question: What is the default sort order if you write 'ORDER BY title' with no direction?
questions.explanation: ORDER BY defaults to ASC (ascending). Writing ORDER BY title is the same as ORDER BY title ASC.

questions.question: Which keyword is used to limit how many rows are returned in MySQL?
questions.explanation: LIMIT N caps the result at N rows. LIMIT OFFSET, N adds pagination.

questions.question: Write a query that returns every column from the actor table.
questions.code: SELECT * FROM actor;
questions.explanation: SELECT * FROM actor; selects every column from the actor table.

questions.question: Write a query that returns first_name and last_name for every actor, ordered by last_name ascending.
questions.code: SELECT first_name, last_name FROM actor ORDER BY last_name ASC;
questions.explanation: Use ORDER BY last_name ASC to sort alphabetically by last name.

questions.question: Write a query that returns the first 5 films ordered by title.
questions.code: SELECT * FROM film ORDER BY title LIMIT 5;
questions.explanation: ORDER BY title puts rows in alphabetical order, LIMIT 5 caps the result at 5 rows.

questions.question: Write a query that returns the distinct ratings used in the film table.
questions.code: SELECT DISTINCT rating FROM film;
questions.explanation: DISTINCT returns each rating value once (G, PG, PG-13, R, NC-17).

questions.question: Return film title and rental_rate, ordered by rental_rate descending, limited to 10 rows.
questions.hint: ORDER BY rental_rate DESC, then LIMIT 10.
questions.code: SELECT title, rental_rate FROM film ORDER BY rental_rate DESC LIMIT 10;
questions.explanation: ORDER BY rental_rate DESC sorts highest price first, LIMIT 10 returns the top 10.

questions.question: Return the second page (rows 11–20) of customers ordered by last_name. Use LIMIT and OFFSET.
questions.code: SELECT customer_id, first_name, last_name FROM customer ORDER BY last_name LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10;
questions.explanation: OFFSET 10 skips the first 10 rows; LIMIT 10 returns the next 10 — i.e. page 2 of a 10-row page.

questions.question: Which query returns the single longest film, breaking ties by title alphabetically?
questions.hint: ORDER BY two columns, then LIMIT 1.
options: SELECT * FROM film ORDER BY length DESC LIMIT 1;
SELECT * FROM film ORDER BY length DESC, title ASC LIMIT 1;
SELECT * FROM film WHERE length = MAX(length);
questions.explanation: ORDER BY length DESC, title ASC sorts longest first and breaks ties alphabetically; LIMIT 1 keeps the top row.

questions.question: A manager wants the 3 cheapest films to rent for a promotion. Which query helps?
options: SELECT title, rental_rate FROM film ORDER BY rental_rate DESC LIMIT 3;
SELECT title, rental_rate FROM film ORDER BY rental_rate ASC LIMIT 3;
SELECT title FROM film WHERE rental_rate = 0 LIMIT 3;
SELECT title, MIN(rental_rate) FROM film LIMIT 3;
questions.explanation: ORDER BY rental_rate ASC puts the cheapest first; LIMIT 3 returns the three lowest-priced films.

questions.question: Which expression labels a film 'Long' when length > 120 and 'Short' otherwise?
options: CASE WHEN length > 120 THEN 'Long' ELSE 'Short' END
questions.explanation: A searched CASE evaluates the condition and returns Long when true, Short otherwise.

questions.question: What does COALESCE(rental_duration, 0) return when rental_duration is NULL?
questions.explanation: COALESCE returns the first non-NULL argument, so a NULL rental_duration becomes 0.

questions.question: Which function returns NULL when two arguments are equal, otherwise the first argument?
questions.explanation: NULLIF(a, b) returns NULL if a = b, otherwise a. Handy to avoid divide-by-zero.

questions.question: Which keyword in MySQL caps the number of rows returned?
questions.explanation: LIMIT caps the number of rows returned regardless of filtering.

questions.question: Show each film title with a price_band column: 'Budget' if rental_rate < 1, 'Standard' if < 3, else 'Premium'.
questions.code: SELECT title, rental_rate, CASE WHEN rental_rate < 1 THEN 'Budget' WHEN rental_rate < 3 THEN 'Standard' ELSE 'Premium' END AS price_band FROM film;
questions.explanation: CASE evaluates the WHEN branches top to bottom and returns the first match; ELSE catches the rest.

questions.question: Marketing wants the 5 longest PG-rated films, longest first, showing only title and length.
questions.hint: Filter on rating, ORDER BY length DESC, LIMIT 5.
questions.code: SELECT title, length FROM film WHERE rating = 'PG' ORDER BY length DESC LIMIT 5;
questions.explanation: WHERE narrows to PG films, ORDER BY length DESC sorts longest first, LIMIT 5 keeps the top 5.

questions.question: Return distinct combinations of rating and rental_duration from the film table.
questions.hint: DISTINCT applies to all listed columns together.
questions.code: SELECT DISTINCT rating, rental_duration FROM film;
questions.explanation: DISTINCT removes duplicate (rating, rental_duration) pairs, returning each unique combination once.

questions.question: List title and replacement_cost, most expensive first, returning the third page of 10 (rows 21-30).
questions.hint: ORDER BY replacement_cost DESC with LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20.
questions.code: SELECT title, replacement_cost FROM film ORDER BY replacement_cost DESC LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20;
questions.explanation: OFFSET 20 skips the first two pages; LIMIT 10 returns rows 21-30 of the descending list.

questions.question: Show customer name and an active_label that reads 'Active' when active = 1 and 'Inactive' otherwise.
questions.hint: IF or CASE on the active column.
questions.code: SELECT first_name, last_name, IF(active = 1, 'Active', 'Inactive') AS active_label FROM customer;
questions.explanation: IF(condition, then, else) is MySQL shorthand for a two-branch CASE.

questions.question: Fill the blank to alphabetize actors by last then first name: SELECT * FROM actor ORDER BY last_name, ___ ;
questions.explanation: ORDER BY accepts multiple columns; first_name breaks ties when last names match.

questions.question: Why might SELECT title, COUNT(*) FROM film fail in strict mode?
options: A non-aggregated column appears alongside an aggregate with no GROUP BY
questions.explanation: In ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY mode, selecting a bare column next to an aggregate without GROUP BY is an error.

questions.question: A clerk needs the customer list as a single display_name column formatted 'LAST, First'.
questions.hint: CONCAT last_name, a comma, then first_name.
questions.code: SELECT CONCAT(last_name, ', ', first_name) AS display_name FROM customer ORDER BY last_name;
questions.explanation: CONCAT builds the formatted string; ORDER BY last_name presents it alphabetically.

questions.question: Which expression returns 1 for R-rated films and 0 for all others?
options: CASE WHEN rating = 'R' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END
questions.explanation: CASE WHEN rating = 'R' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END flags R films as 1 and everything else as 0.

topics.title: Filtering & Operators
topics.description: Master WHERE conditions with AND, OR, NOT, IN, BETWEEN, LIKE and IS NULL using Sakila tables.

questions.question: Which operator tests whether a value is in a list of choices?
questions.explanation: IN (val1, val2, ...) returns true when the column matches any value in the list.

questions.question: Which operator matches text patterns with wildcards % and _?
questions.explanation: LIKE uses % (any chars) and _ (single char) wildcards. Example: WHERE title LIKE 'A%'.

questions.question: Which range operator includes both endpoints?
questions.explanation: BETWEEN x AND y is inclusive on both ends — equivalent to >= x AND <= y.

questions.question: How do you check whether a column has no value?
questions.explanation: Comparing to NULL with = is always UNKNOWN. Use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL.

questions.question: Which condition matches films whose title starts with 'STAR'?
questions.explanation: LIKE 'STAR%' matches anything beginning with 'STAR'. '%' is zero-or-more characters.

questions.question: What does WHERE rating NOT IN ('R','NC-17') return?
options: Films whose rating is anything except R and NC-17
questions.explanation: NOT IN excludes the listed values. Note: rows where rating IS NULL are also excluded.

questions.question: Which condition matches payments between 2 and 5 dollars inclusive?
questions.explanation: BETWEEN 2 AND 5 includes 2 and 5. The bounds must be in low-to-high order.

questions.question: Which condition matches rentals not yet returned?
questions.hint: return_date will be NULL until returned.
questions.explanation: Open rentals have return_date NULL. = NULL is always UNKNOWN; use IS NULL.

questions.question: Which keyword combines two conditions that must both be true?
questions.explanation: AND yields true only when both sides are true.

questions.question: Which operator negates a boolean condition?
questions.explanation: NOT inverts a condition. Example: WHERE NOT (rating = 'R').

questions.question: Which wildcard in LIKE matches zero or more characters?
questions.explanation: % matches any sequence of characters (including empty). _ matches exactly one character.

questions.question: Which LIKE pattern matches any single character?
questions.explanation: _ matches exactly one character. 'A_E' matches 'ACE', 'APE' but not 'ARENA'.

questions.question: Fill the blank: WHERE return_date ___ NULL  -- finds open rentals.
questions.explanation: Use IS NULL (not = NULL) because NULL is never equal to anything, even itself.

questions.question: Which clause checks a value falls within an inclusive range?
questions.explanation: BETWEEN x AND y is inclusive on both ends.

questions.question: List all films with a rating of 'PG' or 'G'.
questions.code: SELECT film_id, title, rating FROM film WHERE rating IN ('PG','G');
questions.explanation: IN ('PG','G') matches either rating, equivalent to rating = 'PG' OR rating = 'G'.

questions.question: List all customers whose first_name starts with the letter 'A'.
questions.code: SELECT customer_id, first_name, last_name FROM customer WHERE first_name LIKE 'A%';
questions.explanation: LIKE 'A%' matches any string starting with A.

questions.question: Find every film with a length between 90 and 120 minutes, ordered by length.
questions.code: SELECT film_id, title, length FROM film WHERE length BETWEEN 90 AND 120 ORDER BY length;
questions.explanation: BETWEEN 90 AND 120 includes 90 and 120. ORDER BY length sorts ascending by length.

questions.question: List all rentals that have not yet been returned.
questions.code: SELECT rental_id, rental_date, customer_id FROM rental WHERE return_date IS NULL;
questions.explanation: Outstanding rentals have NULL return_date. Use IS NULL.

questions.question: Find all R-rated films longer than 2 hours (>120 min).
questions.code: SELECT title, length, rating FROM film WHERE rating = 'R' AND length > 120;
questions.explanation: Both conditions must hold, so we combine them with AND.

questions.question: Find customers whose first_name contains the letters 'AN' (case-insensitive by default in MySQL).
questions.code: SELECT customer_id, first_name, last_name FROM customer WHERE first_name LIKE '%AN%';
questions.explanation: %AN% matches any string with AN anywhere inside. MySQL default collations are case-insensitive.

questions.question: In a WHERE clause, why is 'rating = NULL' never true?
options: Any comparison with NULL using = yields UNKNOWN, not TRUE
questions.explanation: NULL means unknown; = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, so the row is not returned. Use IS NULL.

questions.question: Which condition keeps films that are NOT rated R, including those whose rating is NULL?
questions.hint: NOT IN drops NULLs; handle them explicitly.
questions.explanation: A plain <> 'R' or NOT IN excludes NULL ratings; adding OR rating IS NULL keeps them.

questions.question: Which condition matches films whose title is exactly 5 characters long using LIKE?
questions.explanation: Each _ matches exactly one character, so '_____' (five underscores) matches 5-character titles.

questions.question: Write a condition that is true when amount is NULL OR zero.
questions.explanation: You must test NULL separately with IS NULL, then OR the zero check, because = 0 never matches NULL.

questions.question: Support needs all customers in store 1 who are currently inactive (active = 0).
questions.code: SELECT customer_id, first_name, last_name FROM customer WHERE store_id = 1 AND active = 0;
questions.explanation: AND requires both conditions: the customer belongs to store 1 and is inactive.

questions.question: Find payments made in 2005 for amounts of at least $5, ordered by amount descending.
questions.code: SELECT payment_id, amount, payment_date FROM payment WHERE YEAR(payment_date) = 2005 AND amount >= 5 ORDER BY amount DESC;
questions.explanation: YEAR() extracts the year for filtering; amount >= 5 enforces the threshold; ORDER BY sorts high to low.

questions.question: List films rated G, PG, or PG-13 whose length is outside the 60-180 minute range.
questions.hint: IN for ratings, NOT BETWEEN for length.
questions.code: SELECT title, rating, length FROM film WHERE rating IN ('G','PG','PG-13') AND length NOT BETWEEN 60 AND 180;
questions.explanation: IN matches any of the listed ratings; NOT BETWEEN 60 AND 180 keeps lengths below 60 or above 180.

questions.question: Return each film title with a flag has_special_features that is 'Yes' when special_features is not null, else 'No'.
questions.code: SELECT title, CASE WHEN special_features IS NOT NULL THEN 'Yes' ELSE 'No' END AS has_special_features FROM film;
questions.explanation: CASE tests IS NOT NULL to distinguish populated values from missing ones.

questions.question: What does WHERE first_name LIKE 'J%n' match?
options: Names containing J and n anywhere
Names starting with J and ending with n
questions.explanation: 'J%n' anchors J at the start and n at the end, with any characters between.

questions.question: List actors whose last name is NOT in the set ('SMITH','JOHNSON').
questions.code: SELECT actor_id, first_name, last_name FROM actor WHERE last_name NOT IN ('SMITH','JOHNSON');
questions.explanation: NOT IN excludes the listed last names. Note NULL last names would also be excluded.

questions.question: Which LIKE clause lets you define a character to treat wildcards literally?
questions.explanation: LIKE '100\%' ESCAPE '\' treats % literally. The ESCAPE clause names the escape character.

questions.question: A clerk wants rentals from staff 1 OR 2 that have not been returned.
questions.hint: staff_id IN list AND return_date IS NULL.
questions.code: SELECT rental_id, staff_id, rental_date FROM rental WHERE staff_id IN (1, 2) AND return_date IS NULL;
questions.explanation: IN (1,2) covers either staff member; IS NULL finds outstanding rentals.

questions.question: How is WHERE a = 1 OR a = 2 AND b = 3 evaluated?
questions.explanation: AND has higher precedence than OR, so it groups as a = 1 OR (a = 2 AND b = 3). Use parentheses for clarity.

questions.question: Find customers whose email ends with '@sakilacustomer.org' and whose first_name starts with A or B.
questions.hint: LIKE for the email suffix, plus OR-grouped name prefixes.
questions.code: SELECT customer_id, first_name, email FROM customer WHERE email LIKE '%@sakilacustomer.org' AND (first_name LIKE 'A%' OR first_name LIKE 'B%');
questions.explanation: The % prefix on the email matches any local part; the parenthesised OR keeps A or B first-name prefixes combined with the email condition.

questions.question: Write a single expression that returns the amount, or 0 when amount IS NULL.
questions.explanation: COALESCE(amount, 0) substitutes 0 whenever amount is NULL.

topics.title: Aggregate Functions
topics.description: Summarise data with COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX, GROUP BY and HAVING.

questions.question: Which function counts the number of rows?
questions.explanation: COUNT(*) returns row count. COUNT(col) counts non-NULL values of col.

questions.question: Which function returns the arithmetic mean?
questions.explanation: AVG(col) returns SUM(col)/COUNT(col), ignoring NULLs.

questions.question: Which clause groups rows for aggregation?
questions.explanation: GROUP BY collapses rows that share a key into one row per group, on which aggregates operate.

questions.question: Which clause filters groups produced by GROUP BY?
questions.explanation: HAVING is like WHERE, but it applies to grouped/aggregated rows after GROUP BY.

questions.question: What does COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) return?
options: The number of distinct customer_id values
questions.explanation: COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts how many unique non-NULL values appear in col.

questions.question: Why does COUNT(column) sometimes differ from COUNT(*)?
options: COUNT(column) skips NULL values, COUNT(*) counts all rows
questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) only counts rows where col IS NOT NULL.

questions.question: In a query with GROUP BY rating, which column can you SELECT without aggregating it?
questions.explanation: Non-aggregated columns in SELECT must be in GROUP BY (in strict SQL mode). Here only rating qualifies.

questions.question: Which query returns ratings with more than 100 films?
options: SELECT rating, COUNT(*) FROM film WHERE COUNT(*) > 100 GROUP BY rating;
SELECT rating, COUNT(*) FROM film GROUP BY rating HAVING COUNT(*) > 100;
SELECT rating FROM film GROUP BY rating WHERE COUNT(*) > 100;
SELECT rating, COUNT(*) FROM film GROUP BY rating ORDER BY COUNT(*) > 100;
questions.explanation: Aggregate filters must use HAVING after GROUP BY. WHERE runs before grouping and cannot see COUNT(*).

questions.question: Which function returns the largest value?
questions.explanation: MAX(col) returns the largest non-NULL value of col.

questions.question: Which function returns the smallest value?
questions.explanation: MIN(col) returns the smallest non-NULL value of col.

questions.question: Which function adds numeric values together?
questions.explanation: SUM(col) returns the total of all non-NULL values in col.

questions.question: Fill the blank: SELECT rating, COUNT(*) FROM film ___ rating;
questions.explanation: GROUP BY rating gives one row per rating with its COUNT(*).

questions.question: Which clause filters aggregated groups?
questions.explanation: HAVING filters rows after grouping; WHERE filters before.

questions.question: Which keyword combined with COUNT counts unique values only?
questions.explanation: COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts unique non-NULL values of col.

questions.question: Count how many films are in the film table.
questions.code: SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_films FROM film;
questions.explanation: COUNT(*) returns the total number of rows in the film table.

questions.question: Return the average rental_rate of all films.
questions.code: SELECT AVG(rental_rate) AS avg_rate FROM film;
questions.explanation: AVG(rental_rate) gives the arithmetic mean. NULLs are ignored.

questions.question: Return number of films per rating, ordered by count descending.
questions.hint: GROUP BY rating, then ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC.
questions.code: SELECT rating, COUNT(*) AS film_count FROM film GROUP BY rating ORDER BY film_count DESC;
questions.explanation: GROUP BY rating collapses films into one row per rating; COUNT(*) sizes each group.

questions.question: Find ratings that contain more than 200 films.
questions.code: SELECT rating, COUNT(*) AS film_count FROM film GROUP BY rating HAVING COUNT(*) > 200;
questions.explanation: HAVING filters the grouped rows — keep only ratings with more than 200 films.

questions.question: Show min, max and average payment amount.
questions.code: SELECT MIN(amount) AS min_amt, MAX(amount) AS max_amt, AVG(amount) AS avg_amt FROM payment;
questions.explanation: MIN, MAX, AVG can be combined in a single SELECT with no GROUP BY for whole-table aggregates.

questions.question: List customers who have made more than 30 rentals.
questions.hint: GROUP BY customer_id, then HAVING COUNT(*) > 30.
questions.code: SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS rental_count FROM rental GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 30 ORDER BY rental_count DESC;
questions.explanation: Group rentals by customer_id, then keep groups whose rental count exceeds 30.

questions.question: Which expression counts only R-rated films via conditional aggregation?
options: SUM(CASE WHEN rating = 'R' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
questions.explanation: SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) adds 1 per matching row — the classic conditional count.

questions.question: COUNT(CASE WHEN rating = 'R' THEN 1 END) gives the count of R films because:
options: CASE returns NULL for non-matches and COUNT ignores NULL
questions.explanation: Without ELSE, CASE returns NULL for non-matches; COUNT skips NULLs, so only matches are counted.

questions.question: For each rating, show total films and how many are longer than 120 minutes (a long_films column) using conditional aggregation.
questions.code: SELECT rating, COUNT(*) AS total, SUM(CASE WHEN length > 120 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS long_films FROM film GROUP BY rating;
questions.explanation: Conditional SUM counts only the long films within each rating group while COUNT(*) totals all.

questions.question: Finance wants total revenue and average payment per staff member, ordered by revenue descending.
questions.hint: GROUP BY staff_id with SUM and AVG.
questions.code: SELECT staff_id, SUM(amount) AS revenue, AVG(amount) AS avg_payment FROM payment GROUP BY staff_id ORDER BY revenue DESC;
questions.explanation: Grouping by staff_id lets SUM and AVG report per-staff totals and averages.

questions.question: List each rating with its average film length, but only ratings whose average length exceeds 115 minutes.
questions.code: SELECT rating, AVG(length) AS avg_length FROM film GROUP BY rating HAVING AVG(length) > 115 ORDER BY avg_length DESC;
questions.explanation: HAVING filters on the aggregated AVG(length), which WHERE cannot reference.

questions.question: What does AVG ignore when computing the mean of a column?
questions.explanation: AVG sums non-NULL values and divides by the count of non-NULL values; NULLs are skipped.

questions.question: Compute revenue per month (YYYY-MM) from the payment table, ordered chronologically.
questions.code: SELECT DATE_FORMAT(payment_date, '%Y-%m') AS month, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM payment GROUP BY DATE_FORMAT(payment_date, '%Y-%m') ORDER BY month;
questions.explanation: DATE_FORMAT buckets payments into year-month groups; SUM totals revenue per bucket.

questions.question: Which clause would you add to a GROUP BY query to keep only groups with COUNT(*) >= 5?
questions.explanation: HAVING filters grouped rows; WHERE cannot see COUNT(*).

questions.question: Show the number of distinct films each customer has rented, for customers renting more than 20 distinct films.
questions.hint: COUNT(DISTINCT i.film_id), join through inventory, HAVING.
questions.code: SELECT r.customer_id, COUNT(DISTINCT i.film_id) AS distinct_films FROM rental r INNER JOIN inventory i ON r.inventory_id = i.inventory_id GROUP BY r.customer_id HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT i.film_id) > 20 ORDER BY distinct_films DESC;
questions.explanation: COUNT(DISTINCT film_id) counts unique titles per customer; HAVING keeps the heavy renters.

questions.question: In a query GROUP BY customer_id, which SELECT item is invalid in ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY mode?
questions.explanation: staff_id is neither the grouping key nor wrapped in an aggregate, so it is rejected in strict mode.

questions.question: Across all payments, return counts of small (<2), medium (2-4.99) and large (>=5) payments in one row using conditional sums.
questions.code: SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN amount < 2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS small, SUM(CASE WHEN amount >= 2 AND amount < 5 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS medium, SUM(CASE WHEN amount >= 5 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS large FROM payment;
questions.explanation: Each conditional SUM tallies one band; together they pivot the amount distribution into one row.

questions.question: Find the highest single payment amount recorded for each customer, showing only the top 10 customers by that maximum.
questions.hint: MAX(amount) grouped, ORDER BY it, LIMIT 10.
questions.code: SELECT customer_id, MAX(amount) AS top_payment FROM payment GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY top_payment DESC LIMIT 10;
questions.explanation: MAX(amount) per customer gives their largest payment; ORDER BY + LIMIT surfaces the top 10.

questions.question: Which aggregate would you use to total revenue across all payments?
questions.explanation: SUM(amount) adds every non-NULL payment amount.

questions.question: To compute the percentage of films that are R-rated, which approach works in one query?
options: SUM(CASE WHEN rating = 'R' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*) * 100
questions.explanation: Conditional SUM counts R films; dividing by COUNT(*) and multiplying by 100 yields the percentage.

questions.question: Return per category the total number of films, using the film_category and category tables.
questions.hint: Join then GROUP BY category name.
questions.code: SELECT c.name AS category, COUNT(*) AS film_count FROM film_category fc INNER JOIN category c ON fc.category_id = c.category_id GROUP BY c.name ORDER BY film_count DESC;
questions.explanation: Joining film_category to category and grouping by name gives the film tally per category.

topics.title: JOINs
topics.description: Combine tables with INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, SELF and multi-table joins.

questions.question: Which join returns only matching rows from both sides?
questions.hint: It's the default when you write just JOIN.
questions.explanation: INNER JOIN returns rows where the ON predicate is true on both sides; unmatched rows are dropped.

questions.question: Which join keeps all rows from the left table even if no match exists on the right?
questions.hint: Use NULLs for missing right-side columns.
questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN preserves every left-side row. Unmatched right-side columns appear as NULL.

questions.question: What does ON specify in a JOIN?
options: The join predicate linking the two tables
questions.explanation: ON gives the predicate that decides which rows of the two tables match.

questions.question: Which join joins a table to itself?
questions.explanation: A self join joins a table to itself, usually with two different aliases.

questions.question: What is a Cartesian product produced by?
options: INNER JOIN with an ON clause
CROSS JOIN or JOIN with no condition
questions.explanation: CROSS JOIN (or JOIN without ON) returns every combination of left × right rows — the Cartesian product.

questions.question: To list every customer plus their rentals, including customers with no rentals, you should use:
questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN keeps all rows from customer, even when no matching rental exists.

questions.question: Which junction table connects film and actor in Sakila?
questions.explanation: film_actor (actor_id, film_id) is the M:N bridge between film and actor.

questions.question: Which join returns all rows from both tables, NULLs where no match? (Not natively supported in MySQL.)
questions.explanation: FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both sides. MySQL doesn't support it directly; emulate with UNION of LEFT and RIGHT joins.

questions.question: Which keyword introduces the predicate of a JOIN?
questions.explanation: ON specifies the join predicate. Example: ... JOIN language l ON f.language_id = l.language_id.

questions.question: Which join keeps every row from the right side, NULL for missing left side?
questions.explanation: RIGHT JOIN is the mirror of LEFT JOIN — all right-side rows, plus matching left-side rows.

questions.question: Which keyword joins a table with itself (we name it differently with an alias)?
questions.explanation: A SELF JOIN aliases the same table twice and joins it on a relationship within itself.

questions.question: Which Sakila table links film and category?
questions.explanation: film_category (film_id, category_id) is the M:N bridge between film and category.

questions.question: When using LEFT JOIN, columns from the unmatched right table appear as what?
questions.explanation: Right-side columns are NULL when no matching row exists on the right side.

questions.question: How many JOINs do you need to list film_title and category_name? Use film + film_category + category.
questions.explanation: film → film_category → category requires two JOINs to bridge through the junction table.

questions.question: Return film title and language name for every film.
questions.code: SELECT f.title, l.name AS language FROM film f INNER JOIN language l ON f.language_id = l.language_id;
questions.explanation: Joining film to language on language_id pulls in the language name for each film.

questions.question: List every customer plus the date of each rental. Include customers who have never rented.
questions.code: SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.last_name, r.rental_date FROM customer c LEFT JOIN rental r ON c.customer_id = r.customer_id ORDER BY c.customer_id;
questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN keeps all customers; rental_date is NULL when the customer has no rentals.

questions.question: List film title and actor full name for every film/actor pairing.
questions.code: SELECT f.title, CONCAT(a.first_name, ' ', a.last_name) AS actor_name FROM film f INNER JOIN film_actor fa ON f.film_id = fa.film_id INNER JOIN actor a ON fa.actor_id = a.actor_id ORDER BY f.title;
questions.explanation: film_actor is the junction. Two INNER JOINs walk through it to connect film and actor.

questions.question: List each film with its category name.
questions.code: SELECT f.title, c.name AS category FROM film f INNER JOIN film_category fc ON f.film_id = fc.film_id INNER JOIN category c ON fc.category_id = c.category_id ORDER BY f.title;
questions.explanation: Two INNER JOINs bridge film and category via film_category.

questions.question: Self join staff with itself to list pairs of staff who share the same store_id (no duplicates and no self-pair).
questions.code: SELECT s1.first_name AS staff1, s2.first_name AS staff2, s1.store_id FROM staff s1 INNER JOIN staff s2 ON s1.store_id = s2.store_id AND s1.staff_id < s2.staff_id;
questions.explanation: s1.staff_id < s2.staff_id avoids duplicate pairs and prevents pairing a row with itself.

questions.question: List each customer's total payment amount; include customers with zero payments.
questions.hint: LEFT JOIN payment, then SUM with COALESCE.
questions.code: SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.last_name, COALESCE(SUM(p.amount), 0) AS total_paid FROM customer c LEFT JOIN payment p ON c.customer_id = p.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.last_name ORDER BY total_paid DESC;
questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN keeps customers without payments; COALESCE turns their NULL sum into 0.

questions.question: To find customers who have NEVER rented, which LEFT JOIN pattern works?
questions.hint: Anti-join: filter for NULL on the right side.
options: customer INNER JOIN rental ... WHERE rental_id IS NULL
customer LEFT JOIN rental ON ... WHERE r.rental_id IS NULL
customer RIGHT JOIN rental ... WHERE customer_id IS NULL
questions.explanation: A LEFT JOIN keeps all customers; rows with no matching rental have NULL rental_id, which the WHERE isolates (anti-join).

questions.question: Using an anti-join, list films (title) that are not present in any inventory.
questions.hint: film LEFT JOIN inventory, WHERE inventory_id IS NULL.
questions.code: SELECT f.film_id, f.title FROM film f LEFT JOIN inventory i ON f.film_id = i.film_id WHERE i.inventory_id IS NULL;
questions.explanation: Films with no inventory row get NULL inventory_id after the LEFT JOIN; filtering on that finds the missing ones.

questions.question: Produce a customer directory: full name, city and country for every customer.
questions.code: SELECT CONCAT(c.first_name, ' ', c.last_name) AS customer, ci.city, co.country FROM customer c INNER JOIN address a ON c.address_id = a.address_id INNER JOIN city ci ON a.city_id = ci.city_id INNER JOIN country co ON ci.country_id = co.country_id ORDER BY co.country, ci.city;
questions.explanation: Four tables chain via foreign keys: address holds city_id, city holds country_id.

questions.question: For each store, list staff full name and the city the store is in.
questions.hint: store -> address -> city, plus staff by store_id.
questions.code: SELECT s.store_id, CONCAT(st.first_name, ' ', st.last_name) AS staff, ci.city FROM store s INNER JOIN staff st ON st.store_id = s.store_id INNER JOIN address a ON s.address_id = a.address_id INNER JOIN city ci ON a.city_id = ci.city_id;
questions.explanation: store links to address for its city, and staff links back to store via store_id.

questions.question: When LEFT JOINing payment, how do you treat customers with no payments as having spent 0?
questions.explanation: SUM over no rows yields NULL; COALESCE(SUM(...), 0) converts that to 0.

questions.question: List each customer with rental_status: 'Has rentals' if they appear in rental, else 'No rentals', using a LEFT JOIN.
questions.hint: CASE on whether the right-side key is NULL.
questions.code: SELECT c.customer_id, CASE WHEN r.customer_id IS NULL THEN 'No rentals' ELSE 'Has rentals' END AS rental_status FROM customer c LEFT JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM rental) r ON c.customer_id = r.customer_id;
questions.explanation: The distinct subquery yields one row per renting customer; CASE labels the NULL (non-matching) ones.

questions.question: List films along with how many actors each has, including films with zero actors.
questions.hint: film LEFT JOIN film_actor, COUNT the actor_id.
questions.code: SELECT f.film_id, f.title, COUNT(fa.actor_id) AS actor_count FROM film f LEFT JOIN film_actor fa ON f.film_id = fa.film_id GROUP BY f.film_id, f.title ORDER BY actor_count DESC;
questions.explanation: COUNT(fa.actor_id) counts only matched rows, so films with no actors correctly show 0.

questions.question: Show each payment with the customer name and the staff name who processed it.
questions.code: SELECT p.payment_id, p.amount, CONCAT(c.first_name, ' ', c.last_name) AS customer, CONCAT(s.first_name, ' ', s.last_name) AS staff FROM payment p INNER JOIN customer c ON p.customer_id = c.customer_id INNER JOIN staff s ON p.staff_id = s.staff_id;
questions.explanation: payment carries both customer_id and staff_id, so two INNER JOINs resolve both names.

questions.question: Why might an INNER JOIN return fewer rows than a LEFT JOIN on the same tables?
options: INNER JOIN drops left rows that have no match on the right
They always return the same count
questions.explanation: INNER JOIN keeps only matched pairs; LEFT JOIN additionally keeps unmatched left rows, so it can have more.

questions.question: Find pairs of actors who appeared together in the same film (no duplicate pairs).
questions.hint: Self-join film_actor on film_id with a1.actor_id < a2.actor_id.
questions.code: SELECT fa1.actor_id AS actor_a, fa2.actor_id AS actor_b, fa1.film_id FROM film_actor fa1 INNER JOIN film_actor fa2 ON fa1.film_id = fa2.film_id AND fa1.actor_id < fa2.actor_id;
questions.explanation: Joining film_actor to itself on film_id pairs co-stars; the < condition removes self-pairs and duplicates.

questions.question: Which join type produces every combination of rows from both tables?
questions.explanation: CROSS JOIN yields the Cartesian product: every left row paired with every right row.

questions.question: Show each rental with a returned_flag: 'Returned' when return_date is present, else 'Outstanding'.
questions.code: SELECT r.rental_id, r.rental_date, CASE WHEN r.return_date IS NULL THEN 'Outstanding' ELSE 'Returned' END AS returned_flag FROM rental r;
questions.explanation: CASE inspects return_date; a NULL means the film is still out.

questions.question: List category name and total rental revenue per category.
questions.code: SELECT cat.name AS category, SUM(p.amount) AS revenue FROM category cat INNER JOIN film_category fc ON cat.category_id = fc.category_id INNER JOIN inventory i ON fc.film_id = i.film_id INNER JOIN rental r ON i.inventory_id = r.inventory_id INNER JOIN payment p ON r.rental_id = p.rental_id GROUP BY cat.name ORDER BY revenue DESC;
questions.explanation: The full chain links a category to its films, their inventory, rentals, and the payments those rentals generated.

questions.question: In Sakila, which column joins inventory to film?
questions.explanation: inventory.film_id references film.film_id, linking physical copies to their film.

questions.question: List the title of every film in the 'Action' category.
questions.hint: film -> film_category -> category filtered by name.
questions.code: SELECT f.title FROM film f INNER JOIN film_category fc ON f.film_id = fc.film_id INNER JOIN category c ON fc.category_id = c.category_id WHERE c.name = 'Action' ORDER BY f.title;
questions.explanation: Join through film_category to category and filter on the category name.

topics.title: Subqueries
topics.description: Use scalar, correlated, EXISTS and IN subqueries to express set logic and per-row lookups.

questions.question: A subquery that returns a single value is called:
questions.explanation: A scalar subquery returns one row and one column. It can be used like a value.

questions.question: Which operator tests whether a subquery returns any rows?
questions.explanation: EXISTS (subquery) is true when the subquery returns at least one row.

questions.question: Which keyword tests if a column matches any value returned by a subquery?
questions.explanation: col IN (SELECT ...) is true when col matches at least one value returned by the subquery.

questions.question: What is a correlated subquery?
options: A subquery that references columns from the outer query
A subquery that joins two tables
questions.explanation: Correlated subqueries reference the outer query and are evaluated row-by-row.

questions.question: Which is typically faster on large data: EXISTS or IN — when the inner table has duplicates?
options: EXISTS often performs better because it short-circuits and ignores duplicates
EXISTS only works on small tables
questions.explanation: EXISTS stops at the first match per outer row and is often optimised better when the subquery has duplicates.

questions.question: What does the following return? SELECT * FROM film WHERE length = (SELECT MAX(length) FROM film);
questions.explanation: MAX(length) is a scalar; the outer query keeps films whose length equals that maximum.

questions.question: What's the difference between NOT IN and NOT EXISTS regarding NULL?
questions.hint: NOT IN is unsafe with NULLs.
options: NOT IN can return no rows if the subquery includes any NULL; NOT EXISTS is unaffected
NOT EXISTS only works with one column
questions.explanation: If the NOT IN subquery returns a NULL, the whole comparison becomes UNKNOWN and excludes everything. NOT EXISTS is NULL-safe.

questions.question: Where can a subquery NOT appear?
questions.hint: Trick — it can appear almost anywhere.
options: Inside the GROUP BY of MySQL 8 (it errors)
questions.explanation: Subqueries can appear in SELECT, FROM, WHERE, HAVING and JOINs. GROUP BY accepts expressions, not standalone subqueries.

questions.question: Which keyword starts a subquery you reference as a derived table in FROM?
questions.explanation: Subqueries are just SELECT statements, wrapped in parentheses and given an alias when used in FROM.

questions.question: Which keyword tests if a subquery yields one or more rows?
questions.explanation: EXISTS returns true when the inner query produces at least one row.

questions.question: Which keyword is the negation of EXISTS?
questions.explanation: NOT EXISTS is true when the subquery returns no rows.

questions.question: A subquery that runs once and returns a single value is called a ___ subquery.
questions.explanation: A scalar subquery returns exactly one row, one column — usable wherever a value is expected.

questions.question: A subquery that depends on the outer query's row is called a ___ subquery.
questions.explanation: Correlated subqueries reference outer columns and re-evaluate per outer row.

questions.question: What is a subquery in the FROM clause commonly called?
questions.explanation: A subquery used in FROM (with an alias) is a derived table or inline view.

questions.question: Find every film whose length equals the maximum film length.
questions.code: SELECT film_id, title, length FROM film WHERE length = (SELECT MAX(length) FROM film);
questions.explanation: The scalar subquery returns one value (the longest film length); the outer query filters by it.

questions.question: List customers who have at least one rental.
questions.hint: Use IN with a subquery on rental.
questions.code: SELECT customer_id, first_name, last_name FROM customer WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM rental);
questions.explanation: customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM rental) keeps customers that appear at least once in rental.

questions.question: List customers who have NEVER rented anything. Use NOT EXISTS.
questions.code: SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.last_name FROM customer c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM rental r WHERE r.customer_id = c.customer_id);
questions.explanation: NOT EXISTS returns customers for whom no matching rental row exists. NULL-safe alternative to NOT IN.

questions.question: Show each film with a 'longer_than_avg' flag computed via a scalar subquery.
questions.hint: CASE WHEN length > (SELECT AVG(length) FROM film).
questions.code: SELECT title, length, CASE WHEN length > (SELECT AVG(length) FROM film) THEN 'YES' ELSE 'NO' END AS longer_than_avg FROM film;
questions.explanation: The scalar subquery computes the average once; the CASE compares each film's length to it.

questions.question: For each customer, return their total payment using a correlated subquery in SELECT.
questions.hint: (SELECT SUM(amount) FROM payment p WHERE p.customer_id = c.customer_id).
questions.code: SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.last_name, (SELECT COALESCE(SUM(p.amount), 0) FROM payment p WHERE p.customer_id = c.customer_id) AS total_paid FROM customer c ORDER BY total_paid DESC;
questions.explanation: The correlated subquery runs once per customer, summing that customer's payments.

questions.question: Find the film(s) with the maximum rental_rate within each rating, using a correlated subquery.
questions.code: SELECT f.film_id, f.title, f.rating, f.rental_rate FROM film f WHERE f.rental_rate = (SELECT MAX(f2.rental_rate) FROM film f2 WHERE f2.rating = f.rating) ORDER BY f.rating;
questions.explanation: The correlated subquery returns the max rental_rate for each rating; the outer query keeps films matching it.

questions.question: Which subquery form is safest for 'customers not in the set of renters' when the set may contain NULLs?
questions.hint: NOT IN is unsafe with NULL.
questions.explanation: NOT EXISTS is NULL-safe; NOT IN returns no rows if the subquery yields any NULL.

questions.question: Find films whose rental_rate is above the average rental_rate of their own rating.
questions.code: SELECT f.title, f.rating, f.rental_rate FROM film f WHERE f.rental_rate > (SELECT AVG(f2.rental_rate) FROM film f2 WHERE f2.rating = f.rating);
questions.explanation: The correlated subquery computes the average rate for each row's rating; the outer query keeps above-average films.

questions.question: List customers who have spent more than the overall average customer spend.
questions.hint: Derived table for per-customer totals, compare to its average.
questions.code: SELECT customer_id, total FROM (SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM payment GROUP BY customer_id) AS t WHERE total > (SELECT AVG(amount_sum) FROM (SELECT SUM(amount) AS amount_sum FROM payment GROUP BY customer_id) AS s);
questions.explanation: A derived table builds per-customer totals; another computes the average of those totals to compare against.

questions.question: What does a derived table require that a regular subquery in WHERE does not?
questions.explanation: A subquery used in FROM must be given an alias so the outer query can reference it.

questions.question: Find the film with the second-highest rental_rate using a subquery.
questions.hint: MAX of rates below the overall MAX.
questions.code: SELECT title, rental_rate FROM film WHERE rental_rate = (SELECT MAX(rental_rate) FROM film WHERE rental_rate < (SELECT MAX(rental_rate) FROM film));
questions.explanation: The inner subquery finds the top rate; the middle finds the max strictly below it — the second highest.

questions.question: Label each film 'Above avg' or 'Below/equal avg' based on its length vs the global average length, using a scalar subquery in CASE.
questions.hint: CASE WHEN length > (SELECT AVG(length) FROM film).
questions.code: SELECT title, length, CASE WHEN length > (SELECT AVG(length) FROM film) THEN 'Above avg' ELSE 'Below/equal avg' END AS length_band FROM film;
questions.explanation: The scalar subquery yields the average once; CASE compares each film to it.

questions.question: List actors who appear in more than 30 films, using a subquery count.
questions.hint: IN with a grouped subquery filtered by HAVING.
questions.code: SELECT actor_id, first_name, last_name FROM actor WHERE actor_id IN (SELECT actor_id FROM film_actor GROUP BY actor_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 30);
questions.explanation: The subquery groups film_actor per actor and keeps those with over 30 films; the outer query fetches their details.

questions.question: A correlated subquery is generally evaluated:
options: Once per outer row it references
questions.explanation: Because it references the outer row, a correlated subquery conceptually runs once for each outer row.

questions.question: Find each customer's most recent rental_date using a correlated subquery in the WHERE clause.
questions.code: SELECT r.customer_id, r.rental_id, r.rental_date FROM rental r WHERE r.rental_date = (SELECT MAX(r2.rental_date) FROM rental r2 WHERE r2.customer_id = r.customer_id);
questions.explanation: The correlated subquery returns each customer's latest rental date; the outer query keeps the matching rows.

questions.question: List films that have at least one copy in inventory, using EXISTS.
questions.code: SELECT f.film_id, f.title FROM film f WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM inventory i WHERE i.film_id = f.film_id);
questions.explanation: EXISTS is true as soon as one inventory row matches the film, short-circuiting per film.

questions.question: Which is true of a scalar subquery used in the SELECT list that returns no rows?
questions.explanation: A scalar subquery returning no rows produces NULL in the result column.

questions.question: Find customers whose total spend exceeds that of customer 1, using a scalar subquery for the threshold.
questions.hint: HAVING SUM(amount) > (SELECT SUM(amount) FROM payment WHERE customer_id = 1).
questions.code: SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM payment GROUP BY customer_id HAVING SUM(amount) > (SELECT SUM(amount) FROM payment WHERE customer_id = 1) ORDER BY total DESC;
questions.explanation: The scalar subquery computes customer 1's total once; HAVING compares each group's total to it.

questions.question: List films never rented, using NOT EXISTS through inventory and rental.
questions.hint: NOT EXISTS a rental joined via inventory.
questions.code: SELECT f.film_id, f.title FROM film f WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM inventory i INNER JOIN rental r ON i.inventory_id = r.inventory_id WHERE i.film_id = f.film_id);
questions.explanation: The correlated NOT EXISTS is true when no rented inventory copy of the film exists.

questions.question: Which operator compares a value to every value returned by a subquery (must satisfy all)?
questions.explanation: x > ALL (subquery) is true only if x exceeds every value the subquery returns.

questions.question: WHERE rental_rate > ALL (SELECT rental_rate FROM film WHERE rating = 'G') means:
questions.hint: Greater than the maximum G rate.
options: Greater than the minimum G rate
Greater than every G-rated film's rate (i.e. > the max)
Greater than the average G rate
questions.explanation: > ALL requires the value to beat every element, which is equivalent to being greater than the maximum.

topics.title: String & Date Functions
topics.description: Manipulate text with CONCAT, LENGTH, SUBSTRING, UPPER/LOWER, and work with dates using NOW, DATEDIFF, YEAR, MONTH, DATE_ADD.

questions.question: Which function joins strings together in MySQL?
questions.explanation: CONCAT(a, b, ...) glues strings together. CONCAT_WS adds a separator.

questions.question: Which function returns the character length of a string?
questions.explanation: LENGTH returns byte length; CHAR_LENGTH returns character count (safer with multibyte text).

questions.question: Which function returns the current date and time?
questions.explanation: NOW() returns the current date+time. CURDATE() returns only the date.

questions.question: Which expression extracts the year from rental_date?
questions.explanation: YEAR(date) extracts the year. EXTRACT(YEAR FROM date) is the ANSI equivalent.

questions.question: What does DATEDIFF(return_date, rental_date) return?
options: Days between the two dates (first minus second)
questions.explanation: DATEDIFF returns the difference in days (date1 - date2).

questions.question: Which function returns part of a string starting at position?
options: MID — all three work in MySQL
questions.explanation: MySQL accepts SUBSTRING, SUBSTR and MID as synonyms.

questions.question: Which expression adds 7 days to today?
questions.explanation: DATE_ADD(date, INTERVAL n unit) is the canonical way; NOW() + INTERVAL 7 DAY also works.

questions.question: Which function uppercases a string?
options: UCASE — UPPER and UCASE both work in MySQL
questions.explanation: MySQL has both UPPER() and UCASE() — synonyms.

questions.question: Which function lowercases a string in MySQL?
questions.explanation: LOWER(text) returns the lowercase version. LCASE is a synonym.

questions.question: Which MySQL function returns today's date with no time portion?
questions.explanation: CURDATE() returns the current date (YYYY-MM-DD), no time.

questions.question: Which function removes leading and trailing spaces from a string?
questions.explanation: TRIM(str) removes leading and trailing whitespace by default.

questions.question: Which function returns the month number from a date?
questions.explanation: MONTH(date) returns 1–12.

questions.question: Which function formats a date according to a pattern?
questions.explanation: DATE_FORMAT(date, '%Y-%m-%d') formats dates using format specifiers.

questions.question: Which function returns position of one string inside another?
questions.explanation: LOCATE(substr, str) returns the 1-based position, or 0 if not found. INSTR is an alternative.

questions.question: Build a full_name column for every actor: 'FIRST LAST'.
questions.code: SELECT actor_id, CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name) AS full_name FROM actor;
questions.explanation: CONCAT joins the strings with a literal space in between.

questions.question: Return film title and its character length for every film.
questions.code: SELECT title, CHAR_LENGTH(title) AS title_length FROM film;
questions.explanation: CHAR_LENGTH returns the number of characters in the title.

questions.question: For each rental, compute the number of days the film was kept (NULL if not yet returned).
questions.code: SELECT rental_id, DATEDIFF(return_date, rental_date) AS days_kept FROM rental;
questions.explanation: DATEDIFF returns the day delta. NULL minus anything is NULL.

questions.question: Find rentals whose rental_date falls in July 2005.
questions.hint: Use YEAR and MONTH or BETWEEN.
questions.code: SELECT rental_id, rental_date FROM rental WHERE YEAR(rental_date) = 2005 AND MONTH(rental_date) = 7;
questions.explanation: YEAR()/MONTH() extract parts of the date. BETWEEN '2005-07-01' AND '2005-07-31 23:59:59' is faster on big tables.

questions.question: Return each customer's email in lowercase along with a masked version (first 3 chars + '***').
questions.code: SELECT customer_id, LOWER(email) AS email_lc, CONCAT(SUBSTRING(email, 1, 3), '***') AS masked FROM customer;
questions.explanation: LOWER lowercases; SUBSTRING(str, start, length) extracts characters; CONCAT appends '***'.

questions.question: Compute the expected return date as rental_date + film.rental_duration days.
questions.hint: Join film and use DATE_ADD with INTERVAL.
questions.code: SELECT r.rental_id, r.rental_date, f.rental_duration, DATE_ADD(r.rental_date, INTERVAL f.rental_duration DAY) AS expected_return FROM rental r INNER JOIN inventory i ON r.inventory_id = i.inventory_id INNER JOIN film f ON i.film_id = f.film_id;
questions.explanation: rental → inventory → film gives access to rental_duration; DATE_ADD adds that many days to rental_date.

questions.question: Which function returns its first argument unless it is NULL, in which case the second?
questions.explanation: IFNULL(a, b) returns a when a is not NULL, otherwise b. COALESCE generalizes this to many args.

questions.question: Show each customer's email, replacing NULL emails with the text '(no email)'.
questions.code: SELECT customer_id, COALESCE(email, '(no email)') AS email FROM customer;
questions.explanation: COALESCE substitutes the placeholder string whenever email is NULL.

questions.question: Report the weekday name of each rental_date for rentals in the rental table.
questions.code: SELECT rental_id, rental_date, DAYNAME(rental_date) AS weekday FROM rental;
questions.explanation: DAYNAME returns the textual weekday (Monday, Tuesday, ...) for a date.

questions.question: Group rentals by the day of week and count them, ordered Monday-first.
questions.hint: WEEKDAY for ordering; DAYNAME for label.
questions.code: SELECT DAYNAME(rental_date) AS weekday, COUNT(*) AS rentals FROM rental GROUP BY DAYNAME(rental_date), WEEKDAY(rental_date) ORDER BY WEEKDAY(rental_date);
questions.explanation: WEEKDAY returns 0 for Monday..6 for Sunday, giving the correct ordering while DAYNAME provides the label.

questions.question: Which expression returns the first 3 characters of title?
questions.explanation: LEFT(str, n) returns the leftmost n characters; SUBSTRING(title, 1, 3) is equivalent.

questions.question: Format payment_date as 'DD/MM/YYYY' for display.
questions.code: SELECT payment_id, DATE_FORMAT(payment_date, '%d/%m/%Y') AS display_date FROM payment;
questions.explanation: DATE_FORMAT specifiers %d, %m, %Y build day/month/year in the chosen layout.

questions.question: Find rentals kept longer than the film's allowed rental_duration (late returns).
questions.hint: Compare DATEDIFF to film.rental_duration via inventory join.
questions.code: SELECT r.rental_id, DATEDIFF(r.return_date, r.rental_date) AS days_kept, f.rental_duration FROM rental r INNER JOIN inventory i ON r.inventory_id = i.inventory_id INNER JOIN film f ON i.film_id = f.film_id WHERE r.return_date IS NOT NULL AND DATEDIFF(r.return_date, r.rental_date) > f.rental_duration;
questions.explanation: DATEDIFF gives the days kept; comparing it to the film's rental_duration isolates overdue returns.

questions.question: Which function replaces occurrences of one substring with another?
questions.explanation: REPLACE(str, from, to) swaps every occurrence of the from string with the to string.

questions.question: Show film title and a slug with spaces replaced by underscores.
questions.code: SELECT title, REPLACE(title, ' ', '_') AS slug FROM film;
questions.explanation: REPLACE swaps each space with an underscore to build a simple slug.

questions.question: Which expression counts whole months between two dates regardless of day?
questions.explanation: TIMESTAMPDIFF(MONTH, start, end) returns whole months between the dates, handling year boundaries.

questions.question: List customers and how many full years since their create_date (account age).
questions.code: SELECT customer_id, create_date, TIMESTAMPDIFF(YEAR, create_date, NOW()) AS account_age_years FROM customer;
questions.explanation: TIMESTAMPDIFF with the YEAR unit returns the whole years elapsed between create_date and now.

questions.question: Return each actor's last name padded to 15 characters on the right with dots.
questions.code: SELECT last_name, RPAD(last_name, 15, '.') AS padded FROM actor;
questions.explanation: RPAD pads the string on the right up to the target length using the fill character.

questions.question: NULLIF(amount, 0) is most useful to:
options: Convert 0 to NULL so division by it yields NULL instead of an error
questions.explanation: NULLIF(x, 0) turns 0 into NULL, so x / NULLIF(y, 0) safely returns NULL instead of erroring.

questions.question: Show each customer email with the domain extracted (text after the @).
questions.code: SELECT customer_id, email, SUBSTRING_INDEX(email, '@', -1) AS domain FROM customer WHERE email IS NOT NULL;
questions.explanation: SUBSTRING_INDEX(email, '@', -1) returns everything after the last @ — the domain.

questions.question: Find payments made in the last 7 days relative to the max payment date in the data.
questions.hint: Compare to DATE_SUB of the max date.
questions.code: SELECT payment_id, payment_date, amount FROM payment WHERE payment_date >= DATE_SUB((SELECT MAX(payment_date) FROM payment), INTERVAL 7 DAY);
questions.explanation: DATE_SUB subtracts 7 days from the latest payment date, giving a rolling 7-day window.

topics.title: CRUD Operations
topics.description: INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE rows responsibly — always with a WHERE clause when not bulk-changing.

questions.question: Which statement adds a new row?
questions.explanation: INSERT INTO table (cols) VALUES (...) adds a new row.

questions.question: Which statement modifies existing rows?
questions.explanation: UPDATE table SET col = val WHERE ...; modifies matching rows.

questions.question: Which statement removes rows from a table?
questions.explanation: DELETE FROM table WHERE ...; removes rows. DROP removes the whole table.

questions.question: What happens if you run UPDATE film SET rental_rate = 1.99; (no WHERE)?
options: Every row in film is updated
Only rows where rental_rate is NULL update
questions.explanation: An UPDATE without WHERE applies to every row. Always include WHERE unless you really mean 'all rows'.

questions.question: Which form of INSERT lets you insert from a SELECT?
questions.explanation: INSERT INTO target (cols) SELECT ... FROM source copies rows from one table into another.

questions.question: Which statement empties a table fastest but cannot be filtered?
questions.explanation: TRUNCATE TABLE empties the table quickly and resets AUTO_INCREMENT, but accepts no WHERE.

questions.question: Which clause helps you handle duplicate keys during INSERT in MySQL?
questions.explanation: INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE col = val updates the existing row when a unique key collides.

questions.question: What does the RETURNING clause do (not supported in MySQL but standard in PostgreSQL)?
options: Returns the rows that were modified
questions.explanation: RETURNING outputs modified rows back to the client. MySQL doesn't support it; you need a separate SELECT.

questions.question: Which clause must you almost always include on UPDATE/DELETE for safety?
questions.explanation: WHERE limits the rows affected. Without it, the statement applies to every row.

questions.question: Which keyword starts an INSERT statement?
questions.explanation: INSERT INTO ... VALUES (...) is the standard insert.

questions.question: Which keyword introduces the new values in an UPDATE statement?
questions.explanation: UPDATE table SET col1 = v1, col2 = v2 WHERE ...; SET lists the column assignments.

questions.question: Which statement removes ALL rows quickly without firing per-row triggers?
questions.explanation: TRUNCATE empties the table fast but cannot be filtered and (in MySQL) resets AUTO_INCREMENT.

questions.question: Which statement is used to roll back an open transaction?
questions.explanation: ROLLBACK undoes everything in the current transaction. COMMIT makes it permanent.

questions.question: Which statement makes changes in a transaction permanent?
questions.explanation: COMMIT writes all pending changes in the current transaction to disk.

questions.question: Insert a new actor named 'JANE DOE'. Let actor_id auto-increment, set last_update to NOW().
questions.hint: INSERT INTO actor (first_name, last_name, last_update) VALUES (...).
questions.code: INSERT INTO actor (first_name, last_name, last_update) VALUES ('JANE', 'DOE', NOW());
questions.explanation: Skip actor_id (AUTO_INCREMENT will assign it). last_update is non-null; pass NOW().

questions.question: Change the email of customer_id = 1 to 'mary.smith@example.com'.
questions.hint: UPDATE customer SET email = ... WHERE customer_id = 1;
questions.code: UPDATE customer SET email = 'mary.smith@example.com', last_update = NOW() WHERE customer_id = 1;
questions.explanation: Always include WHERE customer_id = 1 — without it you'd rewrite every customer.

questions.question: Delete rental row rental_id = 99999 only if it is unreturned (return_date IS NULL).
questions.hint: DELETE ... WHERE rental_id = 99999 AND return_date IS NULL;
questions.code: DELETE FROM rental WHERE rental_id = 99999 AND return_date IS NULL;
questions.explanation: Combine the id filter with the return_date check so you can't accidentally delete a returned rental.

questions.question: Increase rental_rate by 0.50 for every PG-13 film.
questions.hint: UPDATE film SET rental_rate = rental_rate + 0.50 WHERE rating = 'PG-13';
questions.code: UPDATE film SET rental_rate = rental_rate + 0.50, last_update = NOW() WHERE rating = 'PG-13';
questions.explanation: Reading and writing the same column in SET is allowed; the original value is used as input.

questions.question: Insert into a backup table actor_archive everything from actor with actor_id < 10. Assume actor_archive already exists with the same columns.
questions.code: INSERT INTO actor_archive (actor_id, first_name, last_name, last_update) SELECT actor_id, first_name, last_name, last_update FROM actor WHERE actor_id < 10;
questions.explanation: INSERT ... SELECT copies rows from one table to another, matching the column lists by position.

questions.question: Within a transaction, deduct $5 from customer 1's next unpaid payment row (amount becomes amount - 5). Use START TRANSACTION and COMMIT.
questions.hint: Wrap the UPDATE in START TRANSACTION; ... COMMIT;
questions.explanation: Wrap the change in START TRANSACTION/COMMIT so it can be rolled back. The inner derived table avoids MySQL's 'update target = subquery target' error.

questions.question: Which UPDATE sets a discount only for films longer than 120 minutes, leaving others unchanged?
questions.hint: CASE inside SET, or a WHERE filter.
options: UPDATE film SET rental_rate = rental_rate * 0.9 WHERE length > 120;
UPDATE film SET length = 120 WHERE rental_rate;
questions.explanation: A WHERE clause limits the discount to long films; other rows are untouched.

questions.question: In one UPDATE, set rental_rate to 4.99 for R films and 2.99 for everything else using CASE.
questions.code: UPDATE film SET rental_rate = CASE WHEN rating = 'R' THEN 4.99 ELSE 2.99 END, last_update = NOW();
questions.explanation: A CASE expression in SET assigns different values per row in a single pass over the table.

questions.question: Deactivate (active = 0) every customer who has never made a payment.
questions.hint: UPDATE ... WHERE customer_id NOT IN (SELECT ... FROM payment).
questions.code: UPDATE customer SET active = 0, last_update = NOW() WHERE customer_id NOT IN (SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM payment);
questions.explanation: The subquery lists paying customers; NOT IN targets those who never paid (safe here because customer_id is never NULL).

questions.question: What is the safest way to preview which rows an UPDATE will affect before running it?
options: Run the UPDATE and check rowcount
Run SELECT * with the same WHERE clause first
questions.explanation: Run a SELECT with the identical WHERE to verify the target rows before mutating data.

questions.question: Insert two new categories ('Documentary HD' and 'Indie') in one statement.
questions.code: INSERT INTO category (name, last_update) VALUES ('Documentary HD', NOW()), ('Indie', NOW());
questions.explanation: A single INSERT can supply multiple VALUES tuples separated by commas.

questions.question: Upsert: insert actor (first ZOE, last QUINN) but if a row with actor_id 201 exists, update its name instead.
questions.code: INSERT INTO actor (actor_id, first_name, last_name, last_update) VALUES (201, 'ZOE', 'QUINN', NOW()) ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE first_name = VALUES(first_name), last_name = VALUES(last_name), last_update = NOW();
questions.explanation: ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE runs the update when the primary/unique key collides; VALUES() refers to the would-be inserted values.

questions.question: Which statement begins an explicit transaction in MySQL?
questions.explanation: START TRANSACTION (or BEGIN) opens a transaction you later COMMIT or ROLLBACK.

questions.question: Raise replacement_cost by 10% for all films in the 'Horror' category.
questions.hint: UPDATE with a subquery on film_category/category.
questions.code: UPDATE film SET replacement_cost = replacement_cost * 1.10, last_update = NOW() WHERE film_id IN (SELECT fc.film_id FROM film_category fc INNER JOIN category c ON fc.category_id = c.category_id WHERE c.name = 'Horror');
questions.explanation: The subquery resolves Horror film_ids; the UPDATE applies the 10% increase only to those.

questions.question: Why can deleting from customer fail with a foreign-key error?
options: Rows in rental/payment reference the customer (FK constraint)
DELETE is not allowed on customer
questions.explanation: Foreign keys in rental/payment point at customer; you must remove or reassign child rows first (or use ON DELETE CASCADE).

questions.question: In a transaction, reduce the latest payment of customer 1 by $3, committing the change.
questions.explanation: Wrapping the change in a transaction lets you ROLLBACK on error; the derived table sidesteps MySQL's self-update restriction.

questions.question: Which statement permanently removes an entire table and its structure?
questions.explanation: DROP TABLE deletes the table definition and all its data; DELETE only removes rows.

questions.question: Update customer active flag to 1 where they have at least one rental and 0 otherwise, in a single statement.
questions.hint: SET active = CASE WHEN EXISTS(...) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END.
questions.code: UPDATE customer c SET active = CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM rental r WHERE r.customer_id = c.customer_id) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END, last_update = NOW();
questions.explanation: The correlated EXISTS drives a CASE that sets active per customer based on rental history.

questions.question: Delete all rentals older than 2005-06-01 that have already been returned.
questions.code: DELETE FROM rental WHERE rental_date < '2005-06-01' AND return_date IS NOT NULL;
questions.explanation: Both conditions ensure only old, already-returned rentals are removed.

questions.question: After TRUNCATE TABLE on an InnoDB table with AUTO_INCREMENT, the next id will be:
questions.explanation: TRUNCATE resets the AUTO_INCREMENT counter, so the next inserted id starts at 1.

questions.question: Copy all inactive customers into customer_archive (assume it exists with columns customer_id, store_id, first_name, last_name, email).
questions.hint: INSERT ... SELECT with a WHERE filter.
questions.code: INSERT INTO customer_archive (customer_id, store_id, first_name, last_name, email) SELECT customer_id, store_id, first_name, last_name, email FROM customer WHERE active = 0;
questions.explanation: INSERT ... SELECT copies the filtered rows; column lists must align by position.

topics.title: Indexes & Performance
topics.description: Speed up queries with indexes, read EXPLAIN plans, and avoid common slow patterns.

questions.question: What does an index primarily improve?
questions.explanation: Indexes speed up SELECTs (and joins) on the indexed columns at the cost of slower writes and more disk space.

questions.question: Which keyword shows the query plan in MySQL?
questions.explanation: Prefix any SELECT with EXPLAIN to see how MySQL plans to execute it.

questions.question: Which is created automatically on a PRIMARY KEY column?
questions.explanation: In InnoDB the PRIMARY KEY is also the clustered index — rows are physically ordered by it.

questions.question: Which common pattern usually prevents an index from being used?
questions.hint: Wrapping the column in a function.
questions.explanation: Wrapping the indexed column in a function (UPPER, DATE, etc.) makes the index unusable unless you have a functional/computed index.

questions.question: A composite index on (a, b, c) helps queries that filter by:
questions.explanation: MySQL can use a composite index only for the leftmost prefix — (a), (a,b), (a,b,c).

questions.question: Which LIKE pattern can still use a B-tree index?
questions.explanation: Only patterns anchored on the left (no leading %) can use a B-tree index.

questions.question: What does 'covering index' mean?
options: An index that covers every column in the table
An index containing all columns needed by the query so no table lookup is required
questions.explanation: If an index includes all columns referenced by the query, MySQL can answer from the index alone (covering index).

questions.question: Which is a downside of adding indexes?
options: Slower INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE and more disk usage
questions.explanation: Indexes must be maintained on every write, so writes get slower and disk usage grows.

questions.question: Which keyword creates a new index?
questions.explanation: CREATE INDEX idx_name ON table(column);

questions.question: Which keyword shows the execution plan?
questions.explanation: EXPLAIN SELECT ...; shows how MySQL will execute the query, including index usage.

questions.question: What's the term for an index that contains every column needed to answer a query?
questions.explanation: A covering index lets MySQL skip reading the row data — the index alone is enough.

questions.question: Which keyword removes an index?
questions.explanation: DROP INDEX idx_name ON table; deletes the index.

questions.question: Which special index in MySQL supports natural-language text search?
questions.explanation: FULLTEXT indexes support MATCH ... AGAINST queries for natural-language search.

questions.question: Which EXPLAIN 'type' value usually indicates a full table scan?
questions.explanation: type=ALL in EXPLAIN means a full table scan — typically the slowest plan.

questions.question: Create a non-unique index named idx_customer_last_name on customer(last_name).
questions.code: CREATE INDEX idx_customer_last_name ON customer(last_name);
questions.explanation: Indexing last_name speeds WHERE last_name = '...' and ORDER BY last_name queries.

questions.question: Inspect the query plan for: SELECT * FROM film WHERE title = 'STAR WARS';
questions.code: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM film WHERE title = 'STAR WARS';
questions.explanation: EXPLAIN shows which indexes are considered/used and the estimated row count.

questions.question: Create a composite index on payment(customer_id, payment_date).
questions.hint: List both columns inside the parentheses.
questions.code: CREATE INDEX idx_payment_customer_date ON payment(customer_id, payment_date);
questions.explanation: Composite index supports WHERE customer_id = ? and WHERE customer_id = ? AND payment_date BETWEEN ... .

questions.question: Drop the index idx_customer_last_name from customer.
questions.code: DROP INDEX idx_customer_last_name ON customer;
questions.explanation: Removes the index. The table data is unaffected.

questions.question: Rewrite this slow query to be index-friendly: SELECT * FROM customer WHERE UPPER(last_name) = 'SMITH'.
questions.hint: Drop the function; use the case-insensitive default collation.
questions.code: SELECT * FROM customer WHERE last_name = 'SMITH';
questions.explanation: MySQL's default collation is case-insensitive, so UPPER() is unnecessary and prevents using an index on last_name.

questions.question: Create a covering index for the query SELECT customer_id, payment_date FROM payment WHERE customer_id = 5 ORDER BY payment_date.
questions.hint: Index on (customer_id, payment_date) covers the query.
questions.code: CREATE INDEX idx_payment_cover ON payment(customer_id, payment_date);
questions.explanation: Both selected columns sit in the index, so MySQL can answer from the index without reading the table.

questions.question: Why does WHERE DATE(rental_date) = '2005-05-25' often skip the index on rental_date?
options: DATE() is not a real function
Wrapping the column in DATE() prevents the optimizer from using the index range
questions.explanation: Applying a function to the indexed column blocks index range scans; use a range like >= and < on the raw column.

questions.question: Rewrite WHERE DATE(rental_date) = '2005-05-25' to be index-friendly using a half-open range.
questions.hint: >= the day AND < the next day.
questions.code: SELECT * FROM rental WHERE rental_date >= '2005-05-25' AND rental_date < '2005-05-26';
questions.explanation: A half-open range on the raw column lets MySQL use an index on rental_date.

questions.question: For ORDER BY customer_id, payment_date, which index avoids a filesort?
questions.hint: Match the sort columns and order.
questions.explanation: A composite index matching the ORDER BY columns in order can satisfy the sort directly, avoiding a filesort.

questions.question: Create an index to speed up lookups of rentals by inventory_id.
questions.code: CREATE INDEX idx_rental_inventory ON rental(inventory_id);
questions.explanation: Indexing inventory_id accelerates joins and filters from inventory into rental.

questions.question: Which EXPLAIN column tells you which index was actually chosen?
questions.explanation: The key column reports the index MySQL decided to use; possible_keys lists candidates.

questions.question: A report filters payment by customer_id and sorts by payment_date, selecting only those two columns. Create a covering index.
questions.hint: Both columns in the index in the right order.
questions.code: CREATE INDEX idx_pay_cust_date_cover ON payment(customer_id, payment_date);
questions.explanation: With both selected columns in the index, MySQL answers from the index alone (covering) and the sort is free.

questions.question: A composite index on (customer_id, payment_date) is LEAST useful for which query?
questions.explanation: Filtering only on payment_date skips the leftmost column, so the composite index cannot be used efficiently.

questions.question: Which keyword enforces uniqueness when creating an index?
questions.explanation: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX prevents duplicate values in the indexed column(s).

questions.question: Ensure no two customers can share the same email by adding a unique index.
questions.code: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_customer_email ON customer(email);
