questions.explanation: A unique index rejects inserts/updates that would duplicate an existing email.

questions.question: Which condition can use an index on last_name?
questions.explanation: Only the left-anchored LIKE 'SM%' (no leading %, no function) can use a B-tree index on last_name.

questions.question: What does a low cardinality column (e.g. active 0/1) imply for indexing?
options: It is always the best index
An index on it is often not selective and may be ignored
questions.explanation: Low-cardinality columns rarely narrow the result much, so the optimizer may prefer a full scan over the index.

questions.question: Show the indexes currently defined on the rental table.
questions.code: SHOW INDEX FROM rental;
questions.explanation: SHOW INDEX FROM table lists every index, its columns, uniqueness and cardinality.

questions.question: Adding many indexes to a write-heavy table primarily risks:
options: Slower INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE due to index maintenance
questions.explanation: Every write must update all relevant indexes, so over-indexing slows down data modification.

questions.question: In EXPLAIN, which type value (besides const/eq_ref) indicates an efficient indexed range lookup?
questions.explanation: type=range means MySQL scans an index over a bounded range — far better than ALL (full scan).

questions.question: Show the EXPLAIN plan for filtering payment by customer_id = 5 to check index usage.
questions.code: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM payment WHERE customer_id = 5;
questions.explanation: EXPLAIN reveals whether the customer_id filter uses an index (key column) or falls back to a full scan (type=ALL).

topics.title: Views & CTEs
topics.description: Build reusable queries with CREATE VIEW and the WITH (CTE) clause.

questions.question: A VIEW is best described as:
options: A named, stored SELECT query you can query like a table
questions.explanation: A view is a stored SELECT. Querying the view runs the underlying SELECT.

questions.question: Which keyword starts a Common Table Expression?
questions.explanation: WITH name AS (SELECT ...) SELECT ... FROM name; defines a CTE for the following query.

questions.question: Which DDL creates a view?
questions.explanation: CREATE VIEW name AS SELECT ...;

questions.question: Which is TRUE about CTEs?
options: They are only visible to the statement that defined them
questions.explanation: A CTE lives for one statement only; views persist in the catalog until dropped.

questions.question: Which keyword introduces a recursive CTE?
questions.hint: Goes between WITH and the name.
questions.explanation: WITH RECURSIVE name AS (anchor UNION ALL recursive_step) ... enables recursion.

questions.question: Can you UPDATE through a simple view in MySQL?
options: Only if the view is built on a single table without aggregates/DISTINCT/GROUP BY
questions.explanation: Updatable views must map cleanly back to underlying rows: single table, no aggregation, etc.

questions.question: Which is a benefit of a view?
options: Hides complex joins behind a simple name
Always faster than the underlying query
questions.explanation: Views encapsulate complex SQL and can restrict columns/rows for security. They don't store data (unless materialised, not in MySQL).

questions.question: Which is TRUE about CTEs vs subqueries in MySQL 8?
questions.hint: Both are scoped to one query.
options: CTEs always materialise; subqueries never do
CTEs can be named and referenced multiple times in the same statement
questions.explanation: CTEs improve readability and can be referenced multiple times within the same SQL statement.

questions.question: Which keyword introduces a CTE?
questions.explanation: WITH cte_name AS (...) defines a named CTE.

questions.question: Which statement removes a view?
questions.explanation: DROP VIEW view_name; removes the view definition.

questions.question: Which combination keyword replaces a view if it already exists?
questions.explanation: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v AS SELECT ...; drops and recreates the view atomically.

questions.question: Which keyword (after WITH) introduces a recursive CTE?
questions.explanation: WITH RECURSIVE allows the CTE to reference itself in the UNION ALL step.

questions.question: Which operator combines the anchor and recursive members of a recursive CTE?
questions.explanation: UNION ALL stacks the anchor with the iterative step. The recursion stops when the step returns no rows.

questions.question: What's the term for a view that physically stores its results (not supported natively in MySQL)?
questions.explanation: Materialised views store query results on disk. MySQL has no built-in support; emulate with summary tables.

questions.question: Create a view called v_long_films that lists film_id, title and length for films longer than 120 minutes.
questions.code: CREATE VIEW v_long_films AS SELECT film_id, title, length FROM film WHERE length > 120;
questions.explanation: The view is just a stored SELECT. Query it like a table: SELECT * FROM v_long_films;.

questions.question: Use a CTE called recent_rentals to list rentals from the last 30 days, then SELECT all of them.
questions.hint: WITH recent_rentals AS (SELECT ... WHERE rental_date >= DATE_SUB(NOW(), INTERVAL 30 DAY)) SELECT ...
questions.code: WITH recent_rentals AS (SELECT * FROM rental WHERE rental_date >= DATE_SUB(NOW(), INTERVAL 30 DAY)) SELECT * FROM recent_rentals;
questions.explanation: The CTE encapsulates the filter; the main query reads from it.

questions.question: Create a view v_customer_total_spend showing customer_id, full_name and SUM(amount).
questions.hint: Join customer + payment, GROUP BY customer.
questions.code: CREATE VIEW v_customer_total_spend AS SELECT c.customer_id, CONCAT(c.first_name, ' ', c.last_name) AS full_name, COALESCE(SUM(p.amount), 0) AS total_spend FROM customer c LEFT JOIN payment p ON c.customer_id = p.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.last_name;
questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN keeps customers with no payments; COALESCE replaces NULL with 0; GROUP BY makes the totals per customer.

questions.question: Replace v_long_films so it includes rating as well.
questions.code: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_long_films AS SELECT film_id, title, length, rating FROM film WHERE length > 120;
questions.explanation: CREATE OR REPLACE updates the view definition without an explicit DROP.

questions.question: Use two CTEs: one for revenue per film, one for top-10 films. Return film_id, title, total_revenue for the top-10 films by revenue.
questions.hint: Chain two CTEs in one WITH clause.
questions.code:
WITH film_revenue AS (
  SELECT i.film_id, SUM(p.amount) AS total_revenue
  FROM payment p
  INNER JOIN rental r ON p.rental_id = r.rental_id
  INNER JOIN inventory i ON r.inventory_id = i.inventory_id
  GROUP BY i.film_id
),
top_films AS (
  SELECT film_id, total_revenue FROM film_revenue ORDER BY total_revenue DESC LIMIT 10
)
SELECT f.film_id, f.title, t.total_revenue
FROM top_films t
INNER JOIN film f ON f.film_id = t.film_id
ORDER BY t.total_revenue DESC;
questions.explanation: Two CTEs separated by commas: film_revenue computes per-film revenue, top_films picks the top 10. The final SELECT joins to film for the title.

questions.question: Use a recursive CTE to generate a sequence of numbers from 1 to 10.
questions.hint: WITH RECURSIVE nums(n) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n+1 FROM nums WHERE n < 10).
questions.explanation: Anchor row is 1; each recursive step adds 1 until n reaches 10, producing 1..10.

questions.question: Create a view v_overdue showing rental_id and customer_id for rentals not yet returned.
questions.hint: CREATE VIEW ... WHERE return_date IS NULL.
questions.code: CREATE VIEW v_overdue AS SELECT rental_id, customer_id, rental_date FROM rental WHERE return_date IS NULL;
questions.explanation: The view encapsulates the outstanding-rental filter so it can be queried like a table.

questions.question: Use a CTE to compute revenue per customer, then return only those above 150 total.
questions.hint: WITH cust_rev AS (...) SELECT ... WHERE total > 150.
questions.explanation: The CTE builds per-customer totals once; the main query filters and orders them.

questions.question: With a CTE of per-customer spend, label each customer Gold (>150), Silver (>50) or Bronze using CASE.
questions.explanation: The CTE isolates the aggregation; CASE assigns a loyalty tier per total.

questions.question: Which is TRUE about referencing a CTE multiple times in one statement?
options: A CTE can be referenced only once
A CTE can be referenced multiple times within the statement that defines it
questions.explanation: A CTE is visible throughout the statement that defines it and may be referenced and joined multiple times.

questions.question: Use two CTEs to compare each rating's average length to the overall average length.
questions.hint: One CTE per-rating avg, one for overall avg, then cross join.
questions.explanation: CROSS JOIN attaches the single overall-average row to each rating so you can compute the difference.

questions.question: Create a view v_film_category that joins film to its category name.
questions.hint: CREATE VIEW joining film_category and category.
questions.code: CREATE VIEW v_film_category AS SELECT f.film_id, f.title, c.name AS category FROM film f INNER JOIN film_category fc ON f.film_id = fc.film_id INNER JOIN category c ON fc.category_id = c.category_id;
questions.explanation: The view hides the two-join lookup so consumers can simply query film + category.

questions.question: A recursive CTE stops recursing when:
options: The recursive member returns no new rows
questions.explanation: Recursion ends when the recursive member produces an empty result (subject to cte_max_recursion_depth as a safety cap).

questions.question: Use a recursive CTE to list the first 7 dates starting from 2005-05-24.
questions.hint: Anchor a date, add INTERVAL 1 DAY each step.
questions.explanation: Each recursive step adds one day until the stop condition, generating a 7-day date series.

questions.question: Which statement lets you query a view's definition text in MySQL?
questions.explanation: SHOW CREATE VIEW view_name returns the stored SELECT that defines the view.

questions.question: Create a view of the top 5 films by length (title, length).
questions.hint: CREATE VIEW with ORDER BY length DESC LIMIT 5.
questions.code: CREATE VIEW v_top5_long AS SELECT title, length FROM film ORDER BY length DESC LIMIT 5;
questions.explanation: Views may include ORDER BY and LIMIT; querying the view returns the five longest films.

questions.question: Why might a view containing GROUP BY be non-updatable?
options: Aggregated rows do not map back to single base-table rows
GROUP BY is not allowed in views
questions.explanation: Updatable views require a one-to-one mapping to base rows; aggregation breaks that, so the view is read-only.

questions.question: Using a CTE, rank customers by total spend and return the top 3 with their rank.
questions.hint: CTE with totals, then a window rank.
questions.explanation: The CTE supplies totals; a window RANK orders by spend and LIMIT keeps the top 3.

questions.question: At minimum, how many times must a CTE be referenced by its defining statement to be useful?
questions.explanation: A CTE must be referenced at least once by the statement that defines it.

questions.question: Create a view v_film_flags adding a length_band column (Short/Medium/Long) to every film.
questions.code: CREATE VIEW v_film_flags AS SELECT film_id, title, length, CASE WHEN length < 60 THEN 'Short' WHEN length <= 120 THEN 'Medium' ELSE 'Long' END AS length_band FROM film;
questions.explanation: The view bakes the CASE classification in, so downstream queries get the band for free.

questions.question: Chain CTEs: compute payments per customer, then the average of those totals, returning customers above that average.
questions.explanation: The first CTE aggregates per customer; the second averages those totals; the final query keeps above-average customers.

topics.title: Window Functions
topics.description: Rank, number and look across rows with ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, LAG, LEAD and PARTITION BY.

questions.question: Window functions are introduced by which clause?
questions.explanation: All window functions take an OVER (...) clause defining the window frame.

questions.question: Which function assigns a unique sequential number per row in the window?
questions.explanation: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) numbers rows 1,2,3,... within each partition. Always unique.

questions.question: What does PARTITION BY do inside OVER(...)?
options: Resets the window function per group
questions.explanation: PARTITION BY divides the rows into groups; window functions start over per partition.

questions.question: How do RANK and DENSE_RANK differ on ties?
options: RANK skips numbers after ties; DENSE_RANK does not
DENSE_RANK skips numbers after ties; RANK does not
questions.explanation: After two rows tied at rank 1, RANK gives the next row 3 (skipping 2); DENSE_RANK gives 2.

questions.question: Which function returns the value of a column from the previous row in the partition?
questions.explanation: LAG(col, n) returns the value from n rows before the current row, within the ordered partition.

questions.question: Which function returns the value from the next row?
questions.explanation: LEAD(col, n) is the mirror of LAG, returning the value from n rows after the current row.

questions.question: Which clause inside OVER (...) controls the order rows are processed by the window function?
questions.explanation: ORDER BY inside OVER tells the window function the order of rows; vital for RANK/ROW_NUMBER/LAG/LEAD.

questions.question: Which is TRUE about window functions vs GROUP BY aggregates?
options: Both collapse rows the same way
Window functions keep every row and add a computed value; GROUP BY collapses rows
Window functions cannot be combined with ORDER BY
questions.explanation: Window functions don't collapse rows — they compute per-row values based on a window of surrounding rows.

questions.question: Which keyword introduces the window definition?
questions.explanation: Every window function uses OVER (...) to define its window.

questions.question: Which window function returns a strictly sequential 1,2,3 numbering within each partition?
questions.explanation: ROW_NUMBER() is unique and continuous per partition.

questions.question: Which window function gives the same rank to ties and skips numbers after ties?
questions.explanation: RANK leaves gaps after ties (1,1,3,...).

questions.question: Which window function gives the same rank to ties but does NOT skip numbers?
questions.explanation: DENSE_RANK assigns 1,1,2,... — no gaps after ties.

questions.question: Which clause inside OVER groups rows so the window restarts per group?
questions.explanation: PARTITION BY splits the rowset into groups; window logic resets per partition.

questions.question: Which window function splits rows into N approximately equal buckets?
questions.explanation: NTILE(N) over an ordered window assigns each row to one of N buckets — useful for quartiles/deciles.

questions.question: List films and their length, plus a row number ordered by length descending.
questions.code: SELECT title, length, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY length DESC) AS rn FROM film;
questions.explanation: ROW_NUMBER() numbers each row 1..N in descending length order.

questions.question: For each rating, rank films by length descending. Show title, rating, length and rank.
questions.hint: Use RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY rating ORDER BY length DESC).
questions.code: SELECT title, rating, length, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY rating ORDER BY length DESC) AS length_rank FROM film;
questions.explanation: PARTITION BY rating restarts ranking per rating; ORDER BY length DESC ranks longest first.

questions.question: For each customer, list their payments with a running total of amount over time.
questions.hint: SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY payment_date).
questions.code: SELECT customer_id, payment_date, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY payment_date) AS running_total FROM payment;
questions.explanation: SUM with PARTITION BY + ORDER BY computes a cumulative sum per customer over time.

questions.question: Show each payment with the previous payment amount for the same customer.
questions.hint: LAG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY payment_date).
questions.code: SELECT customer_id, payment_date, amount, LAG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY payment_date) AS prev_amount FROM payment;
questions.explanation: LAG returns the previous row's amount within the same customer's ordered payments.

questions.question: For each rating, return the top 3 longest films using DENSE_RANK.
questions.hint: Wrap in a CTE and filter by rank <= 3.
questions.explanation: DENSE_RANK in a CTE produces a per-rating rank; the outer query keeps only ranks 1..3.

questions.question: For each payment, show amount, the previous amount, and the difference (current - previous) per customer.
questions.code: SELECT customer_id, payment_date, amount, LAG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY payment_date) AS prev_amount, amount - LAG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY payment_date) AS diff FROM payment ORDER BY customer_id, payment_date;
questions.explanation: LAG fetches the previous payment per customer; subtract from the current amount for the delta. The first row per customer has NULL.

questions.question: Which window expression flags the highest-paid payment per customer as 1?
questions.hint: Compare amount to MAX over the partition.
options: CASE WHEN amount = MAX(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END
questions.explanation: MAX(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) is the per-customer max; the CASE flags rows equal to it.

questions.question: Return only each customer's single most recent payment using ROW_NUMBER in a CTE.
questions.hint: rn = 1 after ORDER BY payment_date DESC.
questions.explanation: ROW_NUMBER orders each customer's payments newest-first; keeping rn = 1 yields the latest per customer.

questions.question: For each rating, return the single longest film (one row per rating) using ROW_NUMBER.
questions.hint: PARTITION BY rating ORDER BY length DESC, keep rn = 1.
questions.explanation: ROW_NUMBER guarantees exactly one row per rating (ties broken by title); rn = 1 picks the longest.

questions.question: What does SUM(amount) OVER () (empty OVER) compute on each row?
options: The grand total of amount across all rows, repeated on every row
questions.explanation: An empty OVER() treats all rows as one window, so every row gets the same grand total.

questions.question: Show each payment's amount as a percentage of that customer's total spend.
questions.code: SELECT customer_id, payment_id, amount, ROUND(amount / SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) * 100, 2) AS pct_of_customer FROM payment;
questions.explanation: The windowed SUM gives each customer's total without collapsing rows, enabling a per-row percentage.

questions.question: Which is required to make LAG/LEAD deterministic?
questions.explanation: LAG/LEAD look at neighbouring rows, which is only meaningful when OVER specifies an ORDER BY.

questions.question: For each customer payment, show whether the amount increased vs the previous payment (Up/Down/Same) using LAG and CASE.
questions.code: SELECT customer_id, payment_date, amount, CASE WHEN amount > LAG(amount) OVER w THEN 'Up' WHEN amount < LAG(amount) OVER w THEN 'Down' ELSE 'Same' END AS trend FROM payment WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY payment_date);
questions.explanation: A named WINDOW clause reuses the partition/order; CASE compares the current amount to the previous one.

questions.question: Assign each film to a length quartile (1-4) using NTILE.
questions.code: SELECT title, length, NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY length) AS length_quartile FROM film;
questions.explanation: NTILE(4) divides the length-ordered films into four roughly equal buckets.

questions.question: To keep only the top-N per group with a window function, you must:
questions.hint: Window functions cannot go in WHERE directly.
options: Put the window function in WHERE
Compute the rank in a subquery/CTE, then filter on it in the outer query
Use HAVING with the window function
questions.explanation: Window functions are evaluated after WHERE, so wrap them in a CTE/subquery and filter the alias outside.

questions.question: Compute a 3-payment moving average of amount per customer ordered by date.
questions.hint: AVG with ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW.
questions.code: SELECT customer_id, payment_date, amount, AVG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY payment_date ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS moving_avg_3 FROM payment;
questions.explanation: The ROWS frame limits the window to the current and two preceding payments, yielding a 3-row moving average.

questions.question: Which window function returns the first value in the ordered window frame?
questions.explanation: FIRST_VALUE(col) OVER (...) returns the first value within the frame.

questions.question: For each payment, show the customer's first-ever payment amount alongside the current amount.
questions.hint: FIRST_VALUE over the customer ordered by date.
questions.code: SELECT customer_id, payment_date, amount, FIRST_VALUE(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY payment_date) AS first_amount FROM payment;
questions.explanation: FIRST_VALUE returns the earliest payment amount in each customer's ordered window.

questions.question: PERCENT_RANK() returns a value in which range?
questions.explanation: PERCENT_RANK() returns (rank - 1)/(rows - 1), a fraction from 0 to 1.

questions.question: Rank customers by total spend using SUM in a CTE then RANK over the totals.
questions.hint: Aggregate first, then window over the aggregate.
questions.explanation: The CTE aggregates per customer first; RANK then orders the totals to produce a spend ranking.

questions.question: For each film, show its DENSE_RANK by length within its rating and flag the top one as 'Longest'.
questions.code: SELECT title, rating, length, CASE WHEN DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY rating ORDER BY length DESC) = 1 THEN 'Longest' ELSE '' END AS flag FROM film;
questions.explanation: DENSE_RANK marks the longest film(s) per rating with rank 1, which the CASE labels.
